title: Short Stuff: Plastic Pink Flamingos
summary: Short Stuff episode on plastic pink lawn flamingos. The hosts cover their origin: sculptor Don Featherstone created them around 1957 for Union Products in Leominster, Massachusetts, as his second assignment after the duck-and-ducklings lawn ornaments. Pink fit the Tiki/Caribbean trend, and they became a suburban working-class status symbol. A 1960s backlash against them gave way to a 1970s revival driven by John Waters and his 1972 film Pink Flamingos, after which gay bars and drag performers adopted them as camp emblems. Later they became associated with pranks, and the hosts argue that putting them up now mocks the earnest taste of earlier owners. The episode also covers Madison, Wisconsin's flamingo prank and 2009 official bird designation, their 1980s sales peak (possibly tied to Miami Vice or the 30th anniversary), a charity flamingo-placement chain, production figures, and the swinger rumor.

segments.title: Introduction and the question of owning pink flamingos
segments.summary: Josh introduces pink plastic lawn flamingos as a yard-art classic and teases the claim that owning one is mean. The hosts set up the topic before the break.

segments.title: Origins: Don Featherstone and Union Products
segments.summary: Sculptor Don Featherstone, working for Union Products in Leominster, Massachusetts, created the flamingo as his second assignment, after the duck-and-ducklings ornaments. Pink suited the Tiki trend, and the flamingos sold well as a suburban status symbol.

segments.title: 1960s backlash and John Waters' 1970s revival
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1960s counterculture backlash against lawn ornaments and their 1970s return, credited to John Waters and his 1972 film Pink Flamingos. The revival made them campy and ironic, and gay bars and drag performers adopted them.

segments.title: Pranks, mocking taste, and the mom jeans comparison
segments.summary: Chuck says the flamingos were revived as pranks that mocked the earnest owners. Josh compares this to the ironic return of mom jeans, and the hosts discuss whether the irony is mean.

segments.title: Madison, the 1980s sales peak, and flamingo trivia
segments.summary: The hosts cover Madison, Wisconsin's flamingo prank, which led to the pink flamingo being named its official bird in 2009. They also note the 1980s sales peak, linked to Miami Vice or the 30th anniversary, and the flamingo chain-letter charity prank.

segments.title: Swinger rumor and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts mention the rumor that a pink flamingo in a yard signals swingers, then close the episode.
